summary.headline: The savings message is the only arm that moves purchase intent (+12.3 points), but respondents accept its bill logic only as a claim to verify, and the comfort message is flat and makes the same $129 feel more expensive.
summary.summary:
These are simulated respondents (LLM agents), so treat this as directional evidence for message testing, not a read on real consumers. Savings is the clear winner: purchase intent rose from 32.0 to 44.4 against the placebo control, appeal and recommend both rose by more than a point, and the share calling the price "fair" went from 12% to 52%. The lift came with heavy skepticism (62% skeptical, up from 36%), and the quotes show why. Respondents keep attacking "minus 18%" and "most homes," and they want to check the savings against their own bill before buying.

Comfort did not work. Purchase intent was flat (-0.7, interval -1.71 to 0.5), appeal and recommend barely moved, and "a bit expensive" rose 23 points to 57%. Its purchase distribution also shifted from "might or might not" toward "probably would not" (+15.8 points). Respondents said the ad never says what it saves, and several reacted to the phone-app and "set it and forget it" language as one more gadget to manage. Before acting on any of this, note that the control quotes mention the $129 price and the 20-minute install, which appear only in ad copy, so the control may not be a clean no-exposure baseline.

arm_comparison.why: The only arm that moves purchase intent: +12.3 points [11.29, 13.49] vs control, with appeal +1.4, recommend +1.2, and the 'fair' price share rising from 12% to 52%. It also converts indifference (61% to 3%) into curiosity (35%). The lift is fragile, though: skepticism rose to 62%, and the 'minus 18%' and 'most homes' claims are the main thing respondents say they would check. Its advantage rests on the bill math holding up when people test it.

Purchase intent is flat (-0.7 [-1.71, 0.5]), and appeal (+0.3) and recommend (+0.1) are too small to matter in practice even though they clear zero. Price moves the wrong way: 'a bit expensive' rises +23.2 points to 57%. The purchase distribution also shifts toward 'probably would not' (+15.8 points [12.06, 19.44]), so it moves some undecided people toward no without changing the mean. Respondents say the ad never says what it saves and treat the app framing as clutter.

segment_notes: Savings effects on purchase intent are positive in all 25 listed segments (+11.7 to +15.3), all FDR-flagged, all with intervals excluding zero and n of at least 30. That supports 'the effect is present in these groups.' It does not support 'this group responds more.' The intervals overlap heavily; for example 65+ is [13.18, 17.48] and 18-29 is [9.31, 13.98]. Do not claim that older or less-educated respondents are the best targets from this data.

Partisan segments respond about equally: Republicans +13.6 (n=311), Democrats +13.2 (n=262), and independents or leaners at similar levels. The bill-savings frame does not look partisan in this sample.
The smallest segments (race=other n=50, race=black n=120) have wide intervals (roughly +8.6 to +18.0 and +8.7 to +14.8). They pass the rules, but treat them as weak evidence.

No segment effects were reported for the Comfort arm, so no Comfort segment claims can be made. Renters and landlord objections appear in quotes only; there is no renter segment effect, so treat that as a hint, not a finding.
surprises: The Comfort price frame raised 'a bit expensive' to 57% (control 34%) even though the price is identical ($129). The framing changes perceived value, not the number.

Control respondents cite the $129 price and the 20-minute install, which appear only in treatment copy. The control may be contaminated, which would shrink the measured treatment effects. Check the exposure logic before trusting the baseline.
Skepticism rose in both treatments, including the winner (36% to 62% in Savings). Lift and distrust came together.
Savings' price-fairness shift is mostly a shift out of 'no idea what it costs' (54% to 10%): the message gave people a price frame, and the verdict followed.
Comfort's purchase mean is flat, but its distribution moved toward 'probably would not.' A mean-only read would miss this.
backfire_risks: 'Minus 18%' is an unsupported number in the copy. Respondents named it as the line to check, and if a real bill does not drop, trust in the brand goes down.

'Most homes save $90 to $150 a year, so it pays for itself in about a year' invites the arithmetic and the 'not my home' objection. A payback claim that a respondent's own bill contradicts is worse than no claim.

Comfort's 'set it from your phone and forget it' and 'warms the house before your alarm' trigger app fatigue and read as a luxury for people with money to spare. For cash-tight respondents, that reads as 'not for us.'
Both treatments push '$129' as the headline cost. Respondents in the lower-income and HS-or-less groups read it as a lot of groceries or a car payment, which sets up the 'I'd wait' response.
Asking people to 'check reviews' or 'ask someone who's had one' is a natural response to skepticism. If the brand has no reviews, that advice works against it.
recommended_edits: Savings headline: replace 'Your heating bill, minus 18%.' with 'Stop paying to heat an empty house.' Test it against the current line. The 18% has no basis shown in this test, and it is the claim respondents say they would check first. If Brightloop has an independently sourced savings figure, cite it in the body copy with the source and the sample; if not, cut the number.

Savings body: replace 'Most homes save $90 to $150 a year, so it pays for itself in about a year.' with 'Savings depend on your home and how often it sits empty. Compare your bill before and after.' If you have a sourced range, use it as 'Households in [source, year] saved [range] a year' rather than 'most homes.' Do not keep an unsourced range.

Savings add a compatibility line in the body: 'Check that it works with your furnace and AC before you buy: [insert compatibility checker or list].' This answers the most common practical question in the transcripts, which is whether it works with their system.

Savings: keep 'Installs in 20 minutes', but qualify it: 'DIY install, about 20 minutes if you're handy.' Respondents treat install time as a positive, but some say they would never get round to installing it.

Comfort: cut 'Set it once from your phone and forget it.' and 'Brightloop warms the house before your alarm goes off and cools it before you pull into the driveway.' Replace with a line that names the savings mechanism, as in the Savings copy: 'Brightloop heats and cools when someone is home, not an empty house.' Or drop the Comfort arm from the next round; it showed no lift and moved price perception the wrong way.

Next round, run a 2x2 to isolate what drives the Savings lift: the '18%' phrasing versus 'Savings depend on your home' crossed with and without the 'pays for itself in about a year' line. That tells you whether the number or the mechanism carries the effect.
caveats: These are simulated LLM respondents built from transcripts or survey answers. Results show how the simulated panel reacts, not how real households will. Do not present them as market research.

The intervals are very narrow for a simulated panel (for example, appeal +1.4 [1.38, 1.48]). That suggests overconfidence in the simulation rather than real precision. Do not read the width of these intervals as sampling certainty.

The full purchase-intent distribution is not reported. The category shifts sum to zero, but the 'probably would' and 'definitely would' levels are missing, so top-box shares cannot be computed. The scale behind the means is not stated either.
Quotes were selected to illustrate themes and are not representative. The per-respondent change values (Δ) are not explained, so do not interpret them as effect sizes.

The control arm may be contaminated: its quotes mention the $129 price and the 20-minute install. If the control already saw product details, the treatment effects are understated, and the baseline comparison needs checking.
Only one savings claim was tested. The test cannot separate the effect of '18%', 'most homes', or 'pays for itself'. It can only say the bundle works in this panel.
Segment effects exist only for the Savings arm. Differences between segments are not tested, and several segments are small (n=50 to 120).
